summaries.example: Imagine a storybook character named Zog who is not real. In ordinary logic, saying “Zog is green” may cause a problem because the name seems to need a real object. Free logic lets us talk about Zog without pretending that Zog exists. Different versions then decide whether the sentence is false, true, or neither true nor false.
summaries.summary: Free logic studies reasoning with names that do not necessarily stand for existing things. In many familiar systems, a name must refer to an object in the domain, usually understood as the group of existing objects. Free logic removes that requirement. It still limits “there exists” and “for every” to the objects counted as existing or defined by a special predicate, often written E!. The main versions differ over sentences containing an empty name. Positive free logic can allow some such atomic sentences to be true, including self-identity in some systems. Negative free logic makes these atomic sentences false. Neutral free logic gives them a third status: they are not simply true or false. The entry also compares free logic with inclusive logic, which allows an empty domain, and describes formal languages, meanings, proof systems, problems, and applications. These applications include definite descriptions, undefined operations such as division by zero, fiction, and logics in which different worlds contain different objects.
key_ideas: Ordinary logic often assumes that every name points to an existing object.
Free logic allows names that may point to nothing, or to something that does not exist.
Quantifiers in free logic range over objects marked by the existence predicate.
Positive, negative, and neutral versions treat sentences with empty names differently.
Free logic can help with fiction, descriptions, partial functions, and changing possible worlds.
summaries.why_it_matters: Free logic gives us careful tools for talking about fictional characters, things that might not exist, descriptions that fail to pick out one object, and expressions whose values can be undefined. It also shows that a small change in a rule about names can affect what counts as a good argument. Studying its different versions helps us see that logic is partly about choosing rules that fit the kind of language or subject we want to understand.

important_terms.definition: A system for reasoning that does not require every name or singular term to stand for something that exists.
A word or expression used to talk about one individual, such as a name or “the tallest tree.”
The special idea or predicate used to mark which things count as existing or being defined.
The objects that a quantifier, such as “something” or “everything,” is allowed to range over.

questions_to_think_about: Should “Zog is green” be false if Zog does not exist, or could it have another truth status?
Why might a story need different rules for what is true in the story and what is true in real life?
What should happen to the expression “1 divided by 0”?
Does saying “every dragon is friendly” tell us that any dragons exist?

summaries.example: Let a be a name for an object that does not exist. In classical first-order logic, the inference from P(a) to ∃xP(x) is supported by the assumption that a denotes something in the domain. Free logic blocks that automatic assumption. In negative free logic, P(a) is false when a is empty; in positive free logic, some empty-termed atoms may remain true; in neutral free logic, such an atom may receive a third value. Thus the same-looking argument depends on the semantic variant.
summaries.summary: Free logic is a family of logics designed to avoid existential presuppositions attached to singular terms. Classical first-order logic generally assumes that every term denotes an element of its domain. Free logic permits terms that are empty, while restricting quantification to the terms or objects designated by an existence or definedness predicate, E!. This changes familiar rules: for example, moving from P(a) to ∃xP(x) requires attention to whether a denotes. The major semantic variants are positive, negative, and neutral. Negative semantics make atoms with empty terms false; positive semantics allow some to be true; neutral semantics assign a third value, with different systems using weak or strong Kleene-style behavior. Supervaluational approaches preserve classical patterns by considering completions of partial interpretations, though they introduce additional complexity and can lack compactness. Free logic is not the same as inclusive logic, which permits an empty domain. The entry also surveys formal languages, Hilbert systems, sequent calculi, and applications. These include definite descriptions, partial and non-strict functions, Kripke models with world-relative domains, fictional discourse, and dual-domain or Meinongian systems. It also examines general anomalies: primitive-predicate dependence, failures of substitutivity for co-extensive expressions, and the difficulty of expressing informative existence conditions with ordinary free quantifiers.
key_ideas: Classical first-order logic normally builds in existential assumptions for singular terms; free logic removes those assumptions.
Free quantifiers are restricted to objects satisfying E!, so unrestricted universal specification and existential generalization must be modified.
Positive, negative, and neutral semantics differ chiefly in the treatment of atomic formulas containing non-denoting terms.
Free logic is distinct from inclusive logic: one concerns empty terms, the other concerns an empty domain.
Proof systems for free logic alter quantifier or identity rules, and recent work uses sequent calculi as well as older axiom systems.

The entry identifies recurring difficulties, including failures of substitution, problems with primitive predicates, and the inability to express substantive sufficient conditions for existence using only inner quantification.
summaries.why_it_matters: Free logic makes explicit assumptions that ordinary logic often leaves hidden. This matters whenever language contains empty names, failed descriptions, undefined operations, fictional names, or terms whose denotation changes across times or possible worlds. Its variants also reveal a broader philosophical choice: should reference failure produce falsity, truth in some cases, or a gap between truth and falsity? The subject therefore connects formal rules with questions about meaning, existence, identity, and the proper analysis of arguments.

important_terms.definition: A first-order logical system whose singular terms are not required to denote objects in the quantifier’s domain.
An expression, such as a name or description, used to refer to one individual, whether or not it denotes an existing object.
A predicate, commonly written E!, that marks the terms or objects over which free quantification ranges; it can be read as existence or definedness.
The objects over which quantifiers range in a model. In free logic, this range is tied to the existence or definedness predicate.
The version of free logic in which atomic formulas containing non-denoting terms are treated as false.
The version in which at least some atomic formulas containing non-denoting terms can remain true.
A family in which formulas involving non-denoting terms can receive a third status besides true and false.
A logic that permits the model’s domain itself to be empty; this issue is separate from whether singular terms can be empty.

questions_to_think_about: Should a true predication about a name guarantee that the name denotes something?
Is a third truth status better than choosing true or false for empty-termed atoms?
Why does the form ∀x(Px → E!x) fail to express a substantive claim about what makes something exist?
How do changing domains in modal or tense logic motivate free logic?
Can one preserve classical reasoning while allowing empty names without arbitrary conventions?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “The dragon in the cave is sleeping,” but there is no dragon in the cave. A usual logic may assume that “the dragon in the cave” names something. Free logic does not make that assumption. One version may call the sentence false, another may allow a sentence with an empty term to be true, and a third may say it is neither true nor false. The logic also asks whether “There is something sleeping” follows. That depends on whether the term is counted as existing.
summaries.summary: Free logic is about reasoning when a singular term may be empty: it may fail to denote an existing object. Classical first-order logic usually assumes that every name or term denotes something in the domain. Free logic rejects that built-in assumption but does not simply let ordinary quantifiers range over everything mentioned. Instead, quantification is limited by a predicate often written E!, understood as existence or definedness. Because empty terms are allowed, standard rules such as moving from a statement about a named object to an existential statement must be handled carefully. Free logic comes in three main forms. Positive free logic allows some atomic claims involving empty terms to be true. Negative free logic makes such claims false. Neutral free logic gives them a third status, often described as neither true nor false. Supervaluational methods try to preserve familiar classical laws by examining possible completions of partial interpretations. The entry distinguishes all of this from inclusive logic, which allows a domain with no objects. It also discusses proof systems and applications to definite descriptions, partial functions such as division by zero, modal and tense settings, and fictional discourse. Finally, it notes problems shared by many free logics, including failures of substitution and the inability of ordinary free quantifiers to express informative claims about what is sufficient for existence.
key_ideas: Free logic questions the common assumption that every singular term must refer to an existing object.
Its quantifiers are restricted by an existence or definedness condition, so familiar inference rules need changes.
The three main variants disagree about the truth status of atomic sentences containing empty terms.
Inclusive logic concerns empty domains, while free logic concerns empty singular terms; the two features can occur separately.
Free logic can be used to analyze descriptions, undefined mathematical operations, fiction, and possible worlds with different domains.
The source also discusses limitations, such as trouble expressing meaningful existence conditions and failures of ordinary substitution principles.
summaries.why_it_matters: We often speak about things that are fictional, missing, undefined, merely possible, or present only at some times. Free logic helps explain how such speech can be represented without quietly assuming that every name refers to a real object. Comparing positive, negative, and neutral versions also teaches an important lesson about philosophy of logic: different rules can be reasonable for different purposes, but each brings its own consequences and difficulties.

important_terms.definition: A kind of logic that allows a name or description to fail to refer to an existing object.
A name or description that is used to refer to one individual, such as “Maya” or “the tallest building.”
A predicate that says whether a term refers to an existing or defined object. The entry often represents it as E!.
The collection of objects considered by a quantifier when it says “something” or “everything.”
A free logic that treats atomic sentences with empty terms as false.
A free logic that permits at least some atomic sentences with empty terms to be true.
A free logic that gives some sentences with empty terms a third status rather than simply true or false.
A logic that allows the domain of a model to contain no objects. This is a different question from whether a name can be empty.

questions_to_think_about: If a name fails to refer, should every sentence containing it be false?
Why might someone prefer a third truth status to a simple true-or-false choice?
Is “Every unicorn is blue” meaningful without there being any unicorns?
How could a changing domain in time or in possible worlds create empty names?
What would be gained by having separate quantifiers for existing and non-existing objects?
